title: Software Architecture Styles
tagline: Compare layered, hexagonal, DDD bounded contexts, event-driven, and monolith vs microservices — and know which style fits which problem.

sections.content:
**Software architecture** is the set of high-level decisions that shape how a system is divided into parts, how those parts depend on each other, and how the system evolves over time. A poor architectural choice rarely causes an outright crash on day one — its damage is subtler and far more expensive: each new feature becomes harder to add, each bug fix risks breaking something elsewhere, and eventually the system becomes so entangled that engineers fear touching it. The right architecture keeps a system flexible in exactly the dimensions it needs to flex.

The term *architectural style* refers to a repeatable high-level pattern for organising components and their relationships. Just as civil engineers choose between steel-frame, concrete-slab, or timber-frame construction based on load requirements and site conditions, software architects choose between layered, hexagonal, event-driven, or service-based styles based on team size, change rate, domain complexity, and scalability targets.

This chapter surveys the five most important styles you will encounter in professional software: **layered architecture** (the universal starting point), **hexagonal / ports-and-adapters** (testability and infrastructure independence), **Domain-Driven Design with bounded contexts** (taming complex domains), **event-driven architecture** (async decoupling at scale), and the **monolith vs microservices** spectrum (deployment and organisational trade-offs). Each section covers the motivation, mechanics, worked examples, real trade-offs, and the conditions under which a style becomes the right choice.

A critical mindset before diving in: these styles are not mutually exclusive. A production system might use hexagonal layout within each bounded context, event-driven communication between contexts, and a modular monolith as its deployment unit. Architecture is about choosing trade-offs deliberately, not selecting a single label and applying it universally.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    LAYERED["Layered\nPresentation → Business → Data"]
    HEX["Hexagonal\nDomain at centre, ports and adapters"]
    DDD["DDD Bounded Contexts\nSubdomains with explicit boundaries"]
    EVT["Event-Driven\nProducers, event bus, consumers"]
    MONO["Modular Monolith\nSingle deployable, internal modules"]
    MICRO["Microservices\nIndependent deployable services"]
    LAYERED -->|"refactored for testability"| HEX
    HEX -->|"applied within each"| DDD
    DDD -->|"contexts communicate via"| EVT
    MONO -->|"selectively decomposed into"| MICRO
sections.caption: Architecture styles are composable. A real system often uses hexagonal layout within bounded contexts while those contexts communicate through events — all deployed as a monolith until the team is large enough to justify microservices.

sections.title: City Planning, City Halls, and City-States
sections.content:
**Layered architecture** is like a well-zoned city. Residential neighbourhoods (the UI) are separate from the commercial district (business logic), which is separate from the industrial zone (databases, file systems). A resident does not interact directly with the sewage plant — they turn on a tap (call a service method). The zones are ordered and each zone depends only on the services of the zone below it. Simple, predictable, and very easy to navigate when the city is small.

**Hexagonal architecture** flips the metaphor: now city hall (the domain) sits at the very centre, and every external service — the power grid (PostgreSQL), the road network (HTTP), the postal service (a message queue) — plugs in via standardised connector sockets (ports). City hall issues contracts specifying what it needs: 'deliver mail in an envelope with a recipient address.' It does not care whether the envelope goes by horse, van, or drone. Swap the delivery adapter without touching city hall at all.

**Domain-Driven Design with bounded contexts** recognises that a country is not one city — it is many autonomous municipalities, each with its own local government, bylaws, and vocabulary. What 'a resident' means to the taxation department is different from what it means to the parks department. Forcing one unified definition on both causes each to be polluted with irrelevant concepts. Better to give each department its own coherent model and provide a diplomatic translation layer at the border.

**Microservices** are full city-states — each with its own government, budget, police force, and power grid. They can evolve independently, elect different leaders (use different technology stacks), and scale their population without affecting each other. But coordination requires formal diplomacy: treaties (API contracts), embassies (API gateways), and couriers (message brokers). A village of 200 people does not need city-state independence — the bureaucracy would consume more effort than the governance problem it solves. Choose city-states only when your 'population' (team size and traffic) genuinely demands it.

sections.title: Layered Architecture — The Universal Default
sections.content:
**Layered architecture** organises code into horizontal strata where each layer serves a distinct concern and may only depend on the layer directly beneath it. The classic three-tier arrangement is:

1. **Presentation layer** — HTTP controllers, CLI commands, WebSocket handlers, GraphQL resolvers. Responsible for parsing input, calling business logic, and formatting output. Contains no business rules.
2. **Business Logic layer** — services, use cases, domain objects. Contains the rules that make your application valuable. Has no knowledge of HTTP, SQL, or any specific technology.
3. **Data Access layer** — repositories, ORM configurations, raw SQL. Responsible for reading and writing persistent state. Translates between the persistence format and the objects the business layer works with.

The dependency rule is strict: Presentation calls Business; Business calls Data. Data never calls Business; Business never calls Presentation. This unidirectional dependency keeps layers independent enough to be tested and replaced.

**Why it works:** Humans think naturally in layers — there is an input/process/output structure to almost every computation. Frameworks like Rails, Laravel, Spring MVC, and NestJS are built around this model. Onboarding a new developer is fast because the structure is universally understood.

**Where it breaks down:** In practice, the business layer often starts importing the ORM entity classes directly — `Order` from TypeORM leaks into service logic — creating implicit coupling between the business rules and the database schema. As the system grows, services accumulate too much responsibility and become 'god classes.' The layer boundary enforces *direction* of dependency but not *granularity*. A large layered application can become just as tangled as no architecture at all, just along different fault lines.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    HTTP["HTTP Controller\n(Presentation)"]
    SVC["OrderService\n(Business Logic)"]
    REPO["OrderRepository\n(Data Access)"]
    DB["PostgreSQL\n(Database)"]
    HTTP -->|"calls"| SVC
    SVC -->|"calls"| REPO
    REPO -->|"queries"| DB
sections.caption: Layered architecture: dependencies flow strictly downward. The controller never imports the repository; the repository never imports the service.

sections.title: Hexagonal Architecture — Testability and Infrastructure Independence
sections.content:
**Hexagonal architecture** (also called *Ports and Adapters*, coined by Alistair Cockburn in 2005) is the natural evolution when layered architecture's infrastructure coupling becomes painful. The central insight is: the domain (business logic) should have *zero* imports from any framework, database driver, or HTTP library. It should know only about its own objects and the interfaces (ports) it needs from the outside world.

**Ports** are interfaces — abstract contracts the domain defines and depends upon. There are two kinds:
- **Driving ports (inbound):** interfaces the domain *exposes* to the outside, through which external actors drive the application (e.g. `OrderService` interface called by an HTTP controller).
- **Driven ports (outbound):** interfaces the domain *requires* from the outside (e.g. `OrderRepository`, `EmailSender`, `PaymentGateway`).

**Adapters** are concrete implementations of ports for specific technologies. The HTTP controller is an adapter for the inbound port. The PostgreSQL repository class is an adapter for the outbound `OrderRepository` port. A SendGrid class is an adapter for `EmailSender`.

**Why this matters for testing:** Because the domain depends only on interfaces, you can supply *in-memory adapters* (simple JavaScript objects that implement the interface) in tests. No database connection required. No network required. The entire domain runs in memory at millisecond speed with deterministic, controllable data.

**Swapping infrastructure:** When you decide to switch from PostgreSQL to MongoDB, or from SendGrid to AWS SES, you write a new adapter. The domain code is untouched. This is the Dependency Inversion Principle (the D in SOLID) applied at the architectural scale.

**The hexagon shape:** Cockburn drew the domain as a hexagon not because six sides are meaningful but to visually break away from the top-to-bottom mental model of layered architecture. Each face of the hexagon can have its own port — the shape conveys that there are *many* possible entry and exit points, all equally valid.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    HTTP["HTTP Adapter\n(inbound)"]
    CLI["CLI Adapter\n(inbound)"]
    PORT_IN["Inbound Port\nOrderService interface"]
    DOMAIN["Domain\nOrderService impl"]
    PORT_OUT["Outbound Port\nOrderRepository"]
    PG["PostgreSQL Adapter\n(outbound)"]
    EMAIL["Email Adapter\n(outbound)"]
    HTTP --> PORT_IN
    CLI --> PORT_IN
    PORT_IN --> DOMAIN
    DOMAIN --> PORT_OUT
    PORT_OUT --> PG
    PORT_OUT --> EMAIL
sections.caption: Hexagonal architecture: the domain sits at the centre, insulated from all infrastructure. Swapping HTTP for gRPC or PostgreSQL for MongoDB means writing a new adapter — the domain is unchanged.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The domain function `createOrderService` takes its dependencies as arguments — this is constructor injection without a framework. In tests we pass simple objects; in production we pass real database and email implementations. The domain code is literally identical in both environments. This is what makes hexagonal architecture so powerful for testing and for long-term infrastructure evolution.

sections.title: Domain-Driven Design and Bounded Contexts — Taming Complexity
sections.content:
**Domain-Driven Design (DDD)**, introduced by Eric Evans in his 2003 book, is an approach for tackling *business domain complexity* — the kind of complexity that arises not from algorithms but from the intricate rules, vocabulary, and relationships of a real business. DDD's most architecturally significant concept is the **Bounded Context**.

**What is a Bounded Context?** It is an explicit boundary within which a particular model is internally consistent and the *ubiquitous language* (shared vocabulary between developers and domain experts) applies without ambiguity. Outside that boundary, the same word may mean something different.

Consider a large e-commerce platform. The word `Product` appears everywhere:
- In the **Catalogue context**: a product has a name, description, photos, and category. A product manager cares about these.
- In the **Inventory context**: a product has a SKU, warehouse location, and stock level. A warehouse manager cares about these.
- In the **Billing context**: a product has a unit price, tax category, and discount rules. An accountant cares about these.
- In the **Shipping context**: a product has weight, dimensions, and hazmat flags. A logistics team cares about these.

If you build one `Product` class to serve all four contexts, it accumulates every attribute from every context. It becomes enormous, inconsistent (a product 'has' a warehouse location — but the catalogue team doesn't care), and any change to the billing rules risks breaking the catalogue display. Every team has to understand the full model even when they only need a slice of it.

**DDD's answer:** let each bounded context own its own `Product` model with only the attributes relevant to that context. The Catalogue has `CatalogueProduct`. Billing has `BillingLineItem`. These are deliberately different types. When information must flow between contexts — for example, when an order is placed in the Order context and must reserve stock in Inventory — an **Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL)** translates between the models without polluting either.

**Ubiquitous language** means the terms used in code (class names, method names, database columns) exactly match the terms used by domain experts in conversation. No translation layer in the developer's head. If a business analyst says 'a shipment is dispatched,' the code has a method called `dispatchShipment`, not `updateOrderStatusToShipped`.

**Strategic DDD patterns for context integration:**
- **Shared Kernel**: two contexts share a small subset of the model. Use carefully — coupling both contexts to changes in the shared part.
- **Customer/Supplier**: one context (upstream) produces data that another (downstream) consumes. The downstream adapts to the upstream, or negotiates a contract.
- **Conformist**: downstream accepts whatever the upstream provides without negotiation.
- **Anti-Corruption Layer**: downstream translates the upstream's model into its own terms via an explicit translation component.
- **Published Language**: contexts communicate via a well-defined, documented schema (e.g. an event schema or API spec) — neither context's internal model leaks to the other.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    CAT["Catalogue Context\nCatalogueProduct\n(name, photos, category)"]
    INV["Inventory Context\nInventoryItem\n(SKU, warehouse, stock)"]
    BILL["Billing Context\nBillingLineItem\n(price, tax, discount)"]
    SHIP["Shipping Context\nShipmentPackage\n(weight, dims, hazmat)"]
    ACL1["Anti-Corruption Layer"]
    ACL2["Anti-Corruption Layer"]
    CAT -->|"order placed"| ACL1
    ACL1 -->|"reserve stock"| INV
    CAT -->|"checkout"| ACL2
    ACL2 -->|"create invoice line"| BILL
sections.caption: Each bounded context owns its model of 'Product' with only the relevant attributes. Anti-Corruption Layers translate between contexts at integration points — keeping each model clean and independently evolvable.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The three context models hold different data about the same real-world entity. The ACL function `billingLineItemFromCatalogueProduct` is the only point of coupling — if the Catalogue changes its internal structure, only the ACL needs updating, not the Billing context itself. This isolation is what allows large teams to work independently on different parts of a complex domain.

sections.title: Event-Driven Architecture — Decoupling Through Messages
sections.content:
**Event-driven architecture (EDA)** organises system behaviour around the *publication and consumption of events* — immutable records of things that happened. Instead of Service A calling Service B directly to trigger downstream work, A publishes an event (`OrderPlaced`, `PaymentProcessed`, `UserRegistered`) to an **event bus** or **message broker** (Apache Kafka, RabbitMQ, AWS SQS/SNS, Google Pub/Sub). Any number of consumers subscribe to events they care about and react independently.

**The core decoupling:** the producer and consumers share *no direct knowledge of each other*. The OrderService publishes `OrderPlaced` and stops. It does not know whether one consumer or ten will react, which consumers exist today, or which consumers will be added next year. This is the **Open/Closed Principle** applied at the architectural level: you can add new consumers without modifying the producer.

**Event types and their semantics:**
- **Domain events:** something meaningful happened in the business (`PaymentAuthorised`, `ShipmentDispatched`). Immutable facts.
- **Commands via messages:** instructions to perform an action (`SendWelcomeEmail`, `ReserveInventory`). Point-to-point, typically one consumer.
- **Integration events:** events that cross bounded context boundaries, using a stable published language so both producer and consumer can evolve independently.

**Delivery guarantees:** Most brokers offer *at-least-once delivery* — a message will be delivered at least once, but possibly more than once in failure scenarios. Consumers must be **idempotent** — processing the same event twice should produce the same result as processing it once. (Example: 'reserve 5 units' is not idempotent; 'set reservation for order X to 5 units' is.)

**Ordering:** Kafka guarantees order within a partition; global ordering across partitions is not guaranteed. Systems that require strict ordering must partition by a relevant key (e.g., `order_id`) so all events for a single order arrive in sequence.

**Eventual consistency:** EDA naturally produces systems where different parts of the application are consistent *eventually* but not necessarily *immediately*. When a user places an order, the inventory might not be decremented until the consumer processes the event 50 milliseconds later. For most business processes this is fine; for others (like double-booking a flight seat) it requires careful design with compensating transactions or sagas.

**When EDA is the right choice:**
- Multiple independent systems need to react to the same business event.
- The producer should not wait for all downstream processing to complete.
- You need the ability to add new consumers without deploying the producer.
- You need event replay for rebuilding read models (Event Sourcing pattern).
- Workflows span multiple services with complex branching and compensation logic (Saga pattern).

sections.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    participant OS as OrderService
    participant BUS as Event Bus
    participant IS as InventoryService
    participant ES as EmailService
    participant AS as AnalyticsService
    OS->>BUS: publish OrderPlaced
    BUS->>IS: deliver OrderPlaced
    BUS->>ES: deliver OrderPlaced
    BUS->>AS: deliver OrderPlaced
    IS-->>IS: reserve stock
    ES-->>ES: send confirmation
    AS-->>AS: log conversion
sections.caption: Event-driven decoupling: OrderService publishes one event and completes. Three independent consumers each react in their own way — adding a fourth consumer requires no change to OrderService or any existing consumer.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The key observation: adding the FraudDetection consumer at the bottom requires no change to OrderService, InventoryService, EmailService, or AnalyticsService. In production, these would be separate processes subscribing to a real broker — the pattern is identical. Each consumer handles its own failures, retries, and processing rates independently.

sections.title: Monolith vs Microservices — The Deployment and Organisation Spectrum
sections.content:
The monolith vs microservices decision is perhaps the most debated architectural choice of the past decade, often generating more heat than light. Understanding the actual trade-offs requires being precise about what each term means.

**Monolith** means a single deployable unit — one process, one database (typically), one codebase. A change to any part requires redeploying the whole thing. Common mis-associations: 'monolith' does not mean 'spaghetti code.' A **modular monolith** has strict internal module boundaries, dependency rules between modules, and potentially separate database schemas — but is still one process. This is the sweet spot that is almost always underrated.

**Microservices** means a collection of small, independently deployable services, each owning its data store and communicating over the network (HTTP, gRPC, or message brokers). 'Small' means different things to different teams — some definitions target 'can be rewritten in two weeks,' others focus on single business capability. The Netflix engineering blog is partly responsible for microservices' popularity, but Netflix had specific constraints (massive team, massive scale, specific failure-isolation needs) that do not generalise.

**What microservices genuinely offer:**
- **Independent deployment:** change and deploy the Payment service without touching Catalogue.
- **Independent scaling:** scale the Image Processing service to 50 instances; keep the Admin service at 1.
- **Technology diversity:** use Python for ML, Go for high-throughput APIs, Node.js for real-time.
- **Team autonomy:** a team can own a service end-to-end — its roadmap, tech choices, and on-call rotation.
- **Failure isolation:** a bug in the Recommendation service does not crash the Checkout service (with proper circuit breakers).

**What microservices cost:**
- **Network calls:** what was a local function call (nanoseconds) becomes an HTTP call (milliseconds) that can fail, time out, or return partial data.
- **Distributed transactions:** coordinating a transaction across three services requires sagas or two-phase commit — vastly more complex than a local database transaction.
- **Operational complexity:** service discovery, health checks, distributed tracing, container orchestration (Kubernetes), secrets management, API gateways — a whole new discipline.
- **Data consistency:** each service has its own database, so joins are either impossible or implemented via data replication/denormalisation, which introduces lag and synchronisation logic.
- **Testing complexity:** a feature that spans three services requires contract testing, integration testing across service boundaries, and sometimes a local Docker Compose environment with six containers.

**The modular monolith as the right default:** For most teams and most applications, the correct starting point is a monolith where each business capability is a well-defined module (`src/billing/`, `src/inventory/`, `src/catalogue/`) with explicit interfaces between them and ideally separate database schemas. This delivers team organisation benefits early. When a specific module genuinely needs independent deployment (it has dramatically different scaling needs, its release cadence is much higher, or its on-call team is distinct), extract *that module* into a service. You will know exactly where the boundary is because you drew it months earlier. The infamous 'distributed monolith' — microservices that are tightly coupled, can only be deployed together, and share a database — is what happens when teams decompose prematurely before understanding their domain boundaries.

flowchart LR
    MM["Modular Monolith
One process
Module A | B | C"]
    MS["Microservices
Service A
Service B
Service C"]
    MM -->|"extract when proven need"| MS
    MM -->|"benefits"| B1["Simple deploy
Simple debug
Low ops cost"]
    MS -->|"benefits"| B2["Indep scaling
Team autonomy
Tech diversity"]
sections.caption: The modular monolith delivers most organisational benefits at minimal operational cost. Microservices extraction should be driven by proven, specific bottlenecks — not anticipated future needs.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Architecture — The Decision Framework
sections.content:
With five styles on the table, how do you choose? The following dimensions drive the decision:

**Domain complexity:** Simple CRUD with few business rules → layered is sufficient. Complex rules with multiple expert vocabulary areas → DDD bounded contexts. If domain experts use different words for the same entity in different departments, that is a signal for separate bounded contexts.

**Team size and structure:** Conway's Law observes that a system's architecture will mirror the communication structure of the team that built it. Five engineers → a monolith is fine. Five teams of ten → bounded contexts almost mandate it, and microservices become viable. If two teams always need to coordinate a single deployment, they are probably sharing a service that should be split.

**Testability requirements:** If the domain is complex enough that fast, thorough tests are essential → hexagonal architecture. The ability to run the entire domain logic in memory without a database is one of the highest-leverage engineering investments possible.

**Change rate and change patterns:** Which parts of the system change most frequently? If the Catalogue changes ten times a week and the Admin panel once a month, deploying both together for every Catalogue change is friction. That asymmetry is a signal to extract.

**Scalability requirements:** Does every part of the system have the same load profile? If the Image Processing pipeline needs 100x more compute than the User Management service, a monolith forces you to scale both together wastefully. Microservices let you scale each independently.

**Operational maturity:** Microservices require mature DevOps: container orchestration, distributed tracing, CI/CD per service, and on-call rotations per service. If your team is still working out how to reliably deploy one service, do not add ten more.

**The practical decision tree:**
1. Start with a **modular monolith** with clear internal module boundaries.
2. Apply **hexagonal architecture** within each module when testability becomes important.
3. Apply **DDD bounded contexts** when different modules have divergent vocabularies and models.
4. Introduce **event-driven communication** between modules/contexts when direct coupling causes brittleness or when you need async workflows.
5. Extract modules into **independent services** only when you have a proven, specific need: a team that can fully own a service, a scaling bottleneck that cannot be solved within the monolith, or a deployment cadence that is incompatible with the rest of the system.

**Historical context:** The term 'hexagonal architecture' was coined by Alistair Cockburn in a 2005 blog post, though the idea circulated earlier. 'Domain-Driven Design' was formalised by Eric Evans in his 2003 book of the same name — the 'blue book.' The microservices term gained mainstream traction around 2014 through Martin Fowler and James Lewis's influential article. Event sourcing and CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) are closely related to event-driven architecture and are often paired with DDD. The 'modular monolith' framing was popularised by architects like Sam Newman as a reaction to teams that prematurely adopted microservices and created distributed monoliths — the worst of both worlds.

**Common misconceptions and interview traps:**

**'Microservices are always more scalable'** — wrong. A well-optimised monolith can serve millions of requests per second. Instagram served 1 billion users with a Python monolith. Scale problems are almost always specific to one component, not the whole system.

**'Hexagonal is just dependency injection'** — partially right, but it is more specific: it mandates that the *domain* has zero infrastructure imports and defines the interfaces (ports) that infrastructure must implement — not just any DI pattern.

**'DDD bounded contexts require microservices'** — wrong. Bounded contexts are a *modelling* concept, not a *deployment* concept. You can have perfectly isolated bounded contexts within a monolith.

**'Event-driven means everything is async'** — not necessarily. Within a bounded context, synchronous calls are fine. Events are most valuable at *context boundaries* where async decoupling reduces coupling.

**The interview question to expect:** 'How would you design a large e-commerce system?' The correct answer does not start with 'I would use microservices.' It starts with 'Let me identify the bounded contexts first, then propose a deployment strategy appropriate to the team size and current scale.'

items: **Layered architecture** organises code into Presentation, Business, and Data layers with strict unidirectional dependencies — the simplest and most universally understood starting point, but prone to infrastructure coupling as complexity grows.

**Hexagonal architecture** places the domain at the centre with zero infrastructure imports; ports are interfaces the domain defines, and adapters implement them for specific technologies — enabling full domain testing without any I/O.

**DDD bounded contexts** recognise that large systems contain multiple subdomains with different vocabularies and models; each context owns its model (e.g. 'Product' means different things in Catalogue vs Billing) and anti-corruption layers translate at context boundaries.

**Event-driven architecture** publishes immutable domain events to a broker; producers and consumers share no direct knowledge of each other — new consumers can be added with zero changes to the producer, at the cost of eventual consistency and idempotency complexity.

**Monolith vs microservices** is a deployment and team-organisation trade-off, not a quality trade-off: start with a modular monolith (one process, clear internal module boundaries), and extract services only when you have a proven, specific need like independent scaling or genuine team autonomy.
**Conway's Law** predicts that your system's architecture will mirror your organisation's communication structure — design both together; a team boundary often signals a correct service boundary.

**These styles compose:** a production system often uses hexagonal layout within each bounded context, event-driven communication between contexts, and all of it deployed as a modular monolith until the team is large enough to justify the operational overhead of independent services.

quiz.question: In layered architecture, which direction must dependencies flow?
options: Data layer imports from Business; Business imports from Presentation
Each layer can freely import from any other layer
Presentation imports from Business; Business imports from Data — but never the reverse
All layers import from a shared global configuration module
quiz.explanation: Layered architecture enforces strict unidirectional dependencies: Presentation → Business → Data. A controller may call a service; a service may call a repository; but a repository must never import from a service or controller. Reversing this dependency creates circular coupling.

quiz.question: What is a 'port' in hexagonal (ports and adapters) architecture?
options: A network TCP port number used by the service
An interface or abstract boundary defining what the domain needs from or exposes to the outside world
A database connection pool configuration object
A Docker container port mapping in docker-compose.yml
quiz.explanation: A port is an interface (abstract contract) — such as `OrderRepository` or `EmailSender`. Adapters implement these interfaces for specific technologies. The domain only knows the port, never the concrete adapter — this is what allows infrastructure to be swapped without touching domain logic.

quiz.question: Why does DDD use separate models for 'Product' in the Billing context vs the Inventory context?
options: To avoid foreign key constraints between databases
Because different subdomains have different relevant attributes and rules — forcing one shared model creates unwanted coupling
Because shared models cause circular import errors in JavaScript
To satisfy microservices requirements for independent deployment
quiz.explanation: Billing needs price and tax category; Inventory needs SKU and warehouse location. Forcing one model to serve both contexts pollutes each with irrelevant fields and tightly couples their evolution — a change to billing logic could break inventory display. Separate models keep each context coherent and independently evolvable.

quiz.question: What is the primary decoupling benefit of event-driven architecture?
options: Events are processed faster than direct HTTP calls in all cases
The producer does not need to know which consumers exist — new consumers can be added without changing the producer
Events are automatically stored and replayed on failure with no extra configuration
Event-driven systems never experience data inconsistency
quiz.explanation: The key benefit is producer-consumer decoupling: the OrderService publishes `OrderPlaced` and knows nothing about who consumes it. Adding an AnalyticsService consumer later requires zero changes to OrderService. This is the Open/Closed Principle applied at the architectural level.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the recommended approach to monolith vs microservices for a new project?
options: Always start with microservices to avoid painful extraction later
Start with a modular monolith and extract services only when specific scaling or autonomy needs are proven
Microservices are always better because they enable independent deployment
Monoliths cannot support multiple developers working simultaneously
quiz.explanation: Premature microservices decomposition multiplies network complexity, distributed transaction difficulty, and operational overhead without proportional benefit. A modular monolith delivers team organisation benefits early; service extraction happens when actual, proven bottlenecks appear — at which point you also know exactly where the boundary should be.

quiz.question: What is an Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) in DDD?
options: A security layer that validates and sanitises all API inputs
A translation component that converts models between bounded contexts without polluting either context's model
A database trigger that prevents invalid data from being inserted
A logging middleware that records all cross-service communication
quiz.explanation: An ACL sits between two bounded contexts and translates models between them. For example, it converts a CatalogueProduct (with name and photos) into a BillingLineItem (with price and tax category) when an order is placed. Each context's model remains clean and independent of the other's internal structure.

quiz.question: What is 'ubiquitous language' in Domain-Driven Design?
options: Code written in a language that runs everywhere, such as JavaScript or WebAssembly
A shared vocabulary used consistently by both developers and domain experts within a bounded context
An international naming convention for REST API endpoints
A design pattern for translating between different programming languages
quiz.explanation: Ubiquitous language is a common vocabulary agreed upon by developers and domain experts within a bounded context. Code class names, method names, and database columns use this exact vocabulary — eliminating the translation layer between 'business speak' and 'tech speak' that causes misunderstandings and bugs.

quiz.question: Why must event consumers in a distributed event-driven system typically be idempotent?
options: Because events are always delivered in the wrong order and must be reprocessed
Because most brokers guarantee at-least-once delivery, meaning the same event may arrive more than once
Because event schemas change frequently and consumers must handle multiple versions
Because idempotency is required by the Kafka protocol specification
quiz.explanation: At-least-once delivery means a broker may re-deliver an event after a failure before the consumer acknowledged it. If processing the event twice causes duplicate side effects (charging a customer twice, reserving double inventory), the system is broken. Idempotent consumers produce the same result regardless of how many times they process the same event.

quiz.question: What is the key advantage of hexagonal architecture's domain having zero imports from framework or database code?
options: The domain runs faster because it has no external dependencies
The entire domain can be tested with in-memory adapters — no database or HTTP server required
It satisfies JavaScript module system circular dependency restrictions
It makes the domain code shorter and easier to read in all cases
quiz.explanation: With in-memory adapters implementing the domain's ports, the full domain logic can be exercised in tests without spinning up a database, a web server, or any external process. Tests run in milliseconds and are deterministic — this is one of the highest-leverage properties a complex system can have.

quiz.question: What does Conway's Law predict about software architecture?
options: Software complexity grows exponentially with team size
A system's architecture will mirror the communication structure of the organisation that built it
Microservices are always more scalable than monoliths for large teams
Every bounded context requires its own independent deployment unit
quiz.explanation: Conway's Law (Melvin Conway, 1967) states: 'organisations which design systems are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organisations.' In practice, if two teams own different modules and rarely communicate, the interface between those modules will be poorly integrated — architecture and team structure must be designed together.
